Employees Who Experience Positive Work Environments Show Higher Morale (Simulated Dataset Experiment)

IT3011 - Theory and Practices in Statistical Modeling | Group Assignment | Simulated Dataset

Group TPSM Project Division

2026-04-19

1 Introduction

1.1 Analytical Statement

“Positive work environment improves employee morale.”

This report investigates whether workplace support factors are associated with higher employee morale. We evaluate support through environment satisfaction, relationship quality, work-life balance, overtime burden, and travel pressure. Morale is measured using job satisfaction, job involvement, performance rating, and retention tendency.

1.2 Dataset Description

We use a simulated HR Employee Attrition dataset in the project directory:

  • File: HR-Employee-Attrition.csv
  • Rows: 1470
  • Source type: Simulated experimental data (derived from a copy of the original HR dataset)

1.3 Variable Structure

Role Variables
Independent (Work Environment) EnvironmentSatisfaction, RelationshipSatisfaction, WorkLifeBalance, OverTime, BusinessTravel
Dependent (Morale) JobSatisfaction, JobInvolvement, PerformanceRating, Attrition (inverse)
Control Variables Age, MonthlyIncome, JobLevel, YearsAtCompany, Gender, Department

1.4 Methodology

The analysis follows three phases:

  1. Descriptive Analytics: summaries, distributions, and visual exploration.
  2. Inferential Analytics: ANOVA, t-tests, proportion tests, variance tests, and correlation tests.
  3. Predictive Analytics: multiple linear regression and Naive Bayes classification.

2.4 Cleaning and Encoding

# Remove identifiers and constant columns that do not carry predictive signal.
drop_cols <- intersect(c("EmployeeCount", "EmployeeNumber", "Over18", "StandardHours"), names(data))
data <- data[, setdiff(names(data), drop_cols)]

# Convert string columns to factors.
char_cols <- names(data)[sapply(data, is.character)]
data[char_cols] <- lapply(data[char_cols], factor)

# Binary encodings for modeling.
data$OverTime_Num <- ifelse(data$OverTime == "Yes", 1, 0)
data$Attrition_Num <- ifelse(data$Attrition == "Yes", 1, 0)
data$Retention_Num <- 1 - data$Attrition_Num

# Ordered labels for plotting and ANOVA readability.
sat_levels <- c("Low", "Medium", "High", "Very High")
data$Environment_F <- factor(data$EnvironmentSatisfaction, levels = 1:4, labels = sat_levels, ordered = TRUE)
data$Relationship_F <- factor(data$RelationshipSatisfaction, levels = 1:4, labels = sat_levels, ordered = TRUE)
data$WorkLife_F <- factor(data$WorkLifeBalance, levels = 1:4, labels = sat_levels, ordered = TRUE)

2.5 Derived Variables and Composite Indexes

# Standardize helper
z <- function(x) as.numeric(scale(x))

# Work environment support index
support_matrix <- cbind(
  z(data$EnvironmentSatisfaction),
  z(data$RelationshipSatisfaction),
  z(data$WorkLifeBalance),
  z(1 - data$OverTime_Num),
  z(ifelse(data$BusinessTravel == "Non-Travel", 2,
           ifelse(data$BusinessTravel == "Travel_Rarely", 1, 0)))
)
data$Support_Index <- rowMeans(support_matrix)

# Morale index
morale_matrix <- cbind(
  z(data$JobSatisfaction),
  z(data$JobInvolvement),
  z(data$PerformanceRating),
  z(data$Retention_Num)
)
data$Morale_Index <- rowMeans(morale_matrix)

# Binary and category targets for classification
data$High_Morale <- ifelse(data$Morale_Index > median(data$Morale_Index), 1, 0)
tertile_breaks <- quantile(data$Morale_Index, probs = c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1))
data$Morale_Category <- cut(data$Morale_Index, breaks = tertile_breaks,
                            labels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"),
                            include.lowest = TRUE)
summary(data$Support_Index)
##     Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
## -1.34052 -0.66940 -0.04248  0.00000  0.60676  1.44112
summary(data$Morale_Index)

3.5 Probability Distribution Fitting

3.5.1 Normal Distribution (Morale Index)

fit_norm_morale <- fitdist(data$Morale_Index, "norm")
ad_morale <- ad.test(data$Morale_Index)

Estimated μ = 0, σ = 0.8025. Anderson-Darling p = < 2.22e-16.

ggplot(data, aes(x = Morale_Index)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 30,
                 fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm,
                args = list(mean = fit_norm_morale$estimate["mean"],
                            sd = fit_norm_morale$estimate["sd"]),
                color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Morale Index with Fitted Normal Distribution",
       x = "Morale Index", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()

3.5.2 Gamma Distribution (Monthly Income)

income_positive <- data$MonthlyIncome[data$MonthlyIncome > 0]
fit_gamma <- tryCatch(
  fitdist(income_positive, "gamma"),
  error = function(e) fitdist(income_positive, "gamma", method = "mme")
)
## <simpleError in optim(par = vstart, fn = fnobj, fix.arg = fix.arg, obs = data,     gr = gradient, ddistnam = ddistname, hessian = TRUE, method = meth,     lower = lower, upper = upper, ...): non-finite finite-difference value [2]>
gof_gamma <- tryCatch(gofstat(fit_gamma), error = function(e) NULL)

Estimated shape = 1.9092, rate = 2.94^{-4}.

ggplot(data.frame(x = income_positive), aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 30,
                 fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_function(fun = dgamma,
                args = list(shape = fit_gamma$estimate["shape"],
                            rate = fit_gamma$estimate["rate"]),
                color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Monthly Income with Fitted Gamma Distribution",
       x = "Monthly Income", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()

3.5.3 Poisson Distribution (Num Companies Worked)

fit_pois <- fitdist(data$NumCompaniesWorked, "pois")

Estimated λ = 2.6932.

obs_df <- as.data.frame(table(data$NumCompaniesWorked))
colnames(obs_df) <- c("x", "Observed")
obs_df$x <- as.numeric(as.character(obs_df$x))
obs_df$Observed <- obs_df$Observed / nrow(data)
obs_df$Expected <- dpois(obs_df$x, lambda = fit_pois$estimate["lambda"])

ggplot(obs_df) +
  geom_col(aes(x = x, y = Observed), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7, width = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x, y = Expected), color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(x = x, y = Expected), color = "red", size = 2.2) +
  labs(title = "NumCompaniesWorked: Observed vs Fitted Poisson",
       x = "Count", y = "Probability") +
  theme_minimal()

3.5.4 Bernoulli Distribution (OverTime)

p_hat <- mean(data$OverTime_Num)

Estimated p (OverTime = Yes) = 0.4823.

bern_df <- data.frame(
  Category = factor(c("No", "Yes"), levels = c("No", "Yes")),
  Observed = c(mean(data$OverTime_Num == 0), p_hat),
  Expected = c(1 - p_hat, p_hat)
)
bern_long <- pivot_longer(bern_df, cols = c(Observed, Expected),
                          names_to = "Type", values_to = "Proportion")

ggplot(bern_long, aes(x = Category, y = Proportion, fill = Type)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "OverTime: Observed vs Fitted Bernoulli",
       x = "OverTime", y = "Proportion") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Observed" = "steelblue", "Expected" = "tomato")) +
  theme_minimal()

4 Inferential Analytics

We use α = 0.05. If p < 0.05, reject H₀.

4.1 ANOVA: Environment Satisfaction

  • H₀: Mean morale is equal across environment satisfaction levels.
  • H₁: At least one level has a different mean morale.
anova_env <- aov(Morale_Index ~ Environment_F, data = data)
env_p <- summary(anova_env)[[1]][["Pr(>F)"]][1]
env_f <- summary(anova_env)[[1]][["F value"]][1]
summary(anova_env)
##                 Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)    
## Environment_F    3  500.9   167.0   549.1 <2e-16 ***
## Residuals     1466  445.8     0.3                   
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Result: F = 549.126, p = < 2.22e-16.

TukeyHSD(anova_env)
##   Tukey multiple comparisons of means
##     95% family-wise confidence level
## 
## Fit: aov(formula = Morale_Index ~ Environment_F, data = data)
## 
## $Environment_F
##                       diff       lwr       upr p adj
## Medium-Low       0.4938146 0.3839170 0.6037122     0
## High-Low         1.1420136 1.0303427 1.2536846     0
## Very High-Low    1.7665284 1.6407705 1.8922864     0
## High-Medium      0.6481990 0.5565964 0.7398017     0
## Very High-Medium 1.2727138 1.1643824 1.3810453     0
## Very High-High   0.6245148 0.5143847 0.7346448     0

summary(anova_rel)
##                  Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)

## Residuals      1466  531.4    0.36

p = < 2.22e-16.

4.4 Two-Sample t-test: OverTime

  • H₀: Mean morale is equal for OverTime = Yes and No.
  • H₁: Mean morale differs by overtime status.
t_over <- t.test(Morale_Index ~ OverTime, data = data)
t_over
## 
##  Welch Two Sample t-test
## 
## data:  Morale_Index by OverTime
## t = 20.217, df = 1466.5, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group No and group Yes is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.6748495 0.8198778
## sample estimates:
##  mean in group No mean in group Yes 
##         0.3604632        -0.3869005

p = < 2.22e-16.

4.5 Two-Proportion Test: High Morale in High vs Low Environment

high_env <- data[data$Environment_F == "Very High", ]
low_env <- data[data$Environment_F == "Low", ]

successes <- c(sum(high_env$High_Morale), sum(low_env$High_Morale))
totals <- c(nrow(high_env), nrow(low_env))
prop_res <- prop.test(successes, totals)
prop_res
## 
##  2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction
## 
## data:  successes out of totals
## X-squared = 382.25, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: two.sided
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.8228357 0.9165218
## sample estimates:
##     prop 1     prop 2

5.1.5 Multicollinearity Check (VIF)

if (length(coef(final_model)) > 1) {
  vif_values <- car::vif(final_model)
  if (is.matrix(vif_values)) {
    vif_df <- data.frame(Variable = rownames(vif_values), vif_values, row.names = NULL, check.names = FALSE)
    vif_df[,-1] <- lapply(vif_df[,-1], function(x) round(as.numeric(x), 3))
  } else {
    vif_df <- data.frame(Variable = names(vif_values), VIF = round(as.numeric(vif_values), 3))
  }
} else {
  vif_df <- data.frame(Note = "Final model contains only an intercept. VIF is not applicable.")
}

5.2 Naive Bayes Classification

5.2.1 Train-Test Split

train_idx <- createDataPartition(data$Morale_Category, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
train_data <- data[train_idx, ]
test_data <- data[-train_idx, ]

5.2.2 Model Training

nb_features <- c("EnvironmentSatisfaction", "RelationshipSatisfaction", "WorkLifeBalance",
                 "OverTime_Num", "JobSatisfaction", "JobInvolvement", "PerformanceRating")
nb_formula <- as.formula(paste("Morale_Category ~", paste(nb_features, collapse = " + ")))

nb_model <- naiveBayes(nb_formula, data = train_data)
nb_model$apriori

5.3 New Employee Prediction

Use this block to input one employee profile and get model-based morale predictions.

# Edit this row to score a new employee profile.
new_employee <- data.frame(
  Age = 35,
  MonthlyIncome = 3500,
  YearsAtCompany = 5,
  JobLevel = 1,
  OverTime = "No",
  BusinessTravel = "Travel_Rarely",
  EnvironmentSatisfaction = 3,
  RelationshipSatisfaction = 3,
  WorkLifeBalance = 3,
  JobSatisfaction = 3,
  JobInvolvement = 3,
  PerformanceRating = 3,
  Gender = "Male",
  Department = "Sales",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Match factor levels with dataset.
factor_cols <- names(data)[sapply(data, is.factor)]
for (col in factor_cols) {
  if (col %in% names(new_employee)) {
    new_employee[[col]] <- factor(new_employee[[col]], levels = levels(data[[col]]))
  }
}

# Derived features used by models.
new_employee$OverTime_Num <- ifelse(new_employee$OverTime == "Yes", 1, 0)
new_employee$Environment_F <- factor(new_employee$EnvironmentSatisfaction,
                                     levels = 1:4, labels = sat_levels, ordered = TRUE)
new_employee$Relationship_F <- factor(new_employee$RelationshipSatisfaction,
                                      levels = 1:4, labels = sat_levels, ordered = TRUE)
new_employee$WorkLife_F <- factor(new_employee$WorkLifeBalance,
                                  levels = 1:4, labels = sat_levels, ordered = TRUE)

# Predictions
pred_morale_index <- as.numeric(predict(final_model, newdata = new_employee))
pred_morale_binary <- ifelse(pred_morale_index > median(data$Morale_Index), "High", "Low")
pred_morale_category <- as.character(predict(nb_model, newdata = new_employee))

model_note <- ifelse(length(coef(final_model)) == 1,
                     "Regression model is intercept-only; score has limited personalization.",
                     "Regression model uses selected predictors from backward AIC.")

pred_tbl <- data.frame(
  Predicted_Morale_Index = pred_morale_index,
  Predicted_Binary_Morale = pred_morale_binary,
  Predicted_Morale_Category_NB = pred_morale_category,
  Note = model_note
)
pred_tbl$Predicted_Morale_Index <- round(pred_tbl$Predicted_Morale_Index, 4)

knitr::kable(pred_tbl, caption = "Prediction for New Employee Row")

6 Conclusion

6.1 Summary of Findings

  • ANOVA: Environment Satisfaction: p = < 2.22e-16 (Significant)
  • ANOVA: Work-Life Balance: p = < 2.22e-16 (Significant)
  • ANOVA: Relationship Satisfaction: p = < 2.22e-16 (Significant)
  • t-test: OverTime: p = < 2.22e-16 (Significant)
  • Proportion test: High vs Low Environment: p = < 2.22e-16 (Significant)
  • Correlation: Support vs Morale: p = < 2.22e-16 (Significant)

6.2 Answer to the Analytical Statement

Final Verdict: The statement is supported in this simulated-dataset experiment.

The statement “Positive work environment improves employee morale” is strongly supported by this simulated dataset and model set. Core inferential tests are statistically significant (Environment ANOVA: p = < 2.22e-16, Work-Life Balance ANOVA: p = < 2.22e-16, Relationship ANOVA: p = < 2.22e-16, and High-vs-Low Environment proportion test: p = < 2.22e-16).

The OverTime t-test and Support-Morale correlation are also statistically significant, and the practical signal is strong overall (Pearson r = 0.8471, regression adjusted R² = 0.9438, Naive Bayes accuracy = 87.5%). Therefore, this analysis provides strong evidence that a positive work environment is associated with higher morale in this simulated scenario.

6.3 Predictive Summary

  • Regression adjusted R²: 0.9438
  • Naive Bayes accuracy: 87.5%
  • Interpretation: Predictive performance is strong, so model-based support for the statement is high in this simulated experiment.

6.4 Limitations

  1. This file uses simulated experimental data, so findings should be used for methodological comparison rather than real-world inference.
  2. Composite indexes use equal weighting, which may not reflect true business importance of each component.
  3. Large samples can make small effects statistically significant.
  4. Naive Bayes assumes conditional independence of features.
  5. Survey-style variables are proxies for complex psychological constructs.
